body: Two hours of sleep and a shower that ran hot for ninety seconds. When Jack comes back into 412 with his towel around his neck, the room has become another country. Laney’s monogrammed laptop is propped against Theo’s mirror at full volume, Jay Sean’s falsetto and then Lil Wayne under it, loud enough to go through two floors.
“It’s for 217,” Laney says, by way of good morning. Two floors down. “A diplomatic gesture. Lil Wayne is a *New Orleans* boy. It’s an olive branch with a *beat*.”

She isn’t at the mirror. She’s at Theo’s desk in Theo’s navy silk robe, her hair up in one of his towels, and Theo is beside her in the black Meridian one, their heads together over a yellow legal pad. Theo turns the pad face down with one finger. He doesn’t hurry; Theo never hurries anything he can do beautifully instead. Jack reads two words upside down before it goes over: HALLOWEEN, and under it, underlined twice, SEATING.
“Are you two —”
“No.” Both of them, at once, in harmony.
Laney floats back to the mirror. On the laptop, behind the music, her Facebook is open to her own wall.

body.name: Laney Price
body.text: is a political refugee on the fourth floor. Donations of concealer gratefully accepted.

body: She starts on her face: a sponge, a little bottle, the freckles going under one patch of cheek at a time.

Kevin appears in the doorway with his orgo cards rubber-banded in four colors and a shaker bottle of something the color of wet cement. He takes in the Aerobed, the navy silk, a second toothbrush standing in Theo’s Harvard-Westlake mug. “This,” Kevin says, “is a fire code violation and a cry for help.”
“I’m a *refugee*, Kevin.”
“From the second floor.”

“From *tyranny*.” She points the sponge at him. Since Kevin asked — he didn’t — it was a *game*. The Madonna Inn, the pink booth, everybody laughing, the tin right there in the cardigan pocket. “And she says I went in her *pocket*. In front of *him*.” The sponge swings around to Jack, as if he were the one who had driven in from New Orleans. “I went in a *cardigan*. Technically it was *my* cardigan for the afternoon.”

That is the account, start to finish. Theo pulls her an espresso on the machine Jack is not permitted to touch — the Post-it on it still reads *+ 1 MALIBU —T.V.* — and sets the cup at her elbow on a saucer he got from somewhere, because Theo owns saucers.
Laney finds Jack’s reflection in the mirror and holds it while she does her lip liner. “And for Halloween, sugar, about Idaho — I have *ideas* —”
“No.”
“You haven’t even —”
“No.”

journal.title: Laney’s advice
journal.text: Laney Price, on romance: a poem, out loud, at a bonfire, about her eyes. It has to rhyme. And then — this is the important part — one knee. Not asking her again. I did the knee. Becca said: Not yet. Halloween: No.

response: “There’s no chart,” Theo says.
“There’s *no chart*,” says Laney, to her lip liner.
Theo sets his coffee cup down on the back of the legal pad, square in the middle of the cardboard, and leaves it there like a paperweight on a treaty.
Jack gets his other shoe on and goes out for his nine-thirty with his hair still wet, and Lil Wayne follows him down the hall as far as the stairwell.
The sponge stops on her cheekbone. In the mirror Laney isn’t performing anything for a second; she’s a girl in a borrowed robe with half her freckles showing.
“She doesn’t want to talk to me,” she says. “She wants to be mad at somebody, and I was closest.”
Then the lip liner again, one steady line, and the music, as if she hadn’t said a thing.

response: Laney blows him a kiss in the mirror, a big one, both lips.
Theo doesn’t look up from the cardboard back of the legal pad. “She isn’t a houseguest,” he says. “She’s a sovereign nation.”
Jack gets his other shoe on and goes out for his nine-thirty with his hair still wet, and Lil Wayne follows him down the hall as far as the stairwell.

body: Hollis 302 smells like wet wool and radiator. The storm has scoured the sea window to a gray-green with whitecaps out past the kelp, and down in the cloister it has stripped the bougainvillea and pasted it to the flagstones in magenta fistfuls. The radiator knocks twice, the way it does, a janitor at the door of a meeting. Midterm week: half the table hasn’t slept. Caleb’s *Consolations* is shedding Post-its onto the oak faster than usual. Yusuf has a steel thermos of tea and has drawn a small bridge in his margin, with arrows.
Hale is in his chair before any of them again — the second time this term — with the roster squared in front of him and his hands folded on top of it.

Lena comes in at a minute to one. A dark skirt and the Justins, the green sweatshirt under the oatmeal cardigan, its cuffs hanging out past the cardigan’s. She takes the chair across from Jack, which is hers, and squares her paper to the edge of the table, and looks at him for the first time since the overhang.
“Good afternoon, Mr. Costigan.”
Six weeks across this table, and she has never once called him that.
Hale’s head comes up from the roster. “Mr. Costigan has been demoted,” he says, to the table at large. “How interesting.”

Then the titles. “‘That a Man Can Know His Own Heart.’ Mr. Costigan. ‘That He Cannot.’ Miss Broussard.” He reads the text off a single sheet without needing to look down much. “Jeremiah, seventeen. *The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately corrupt; who can understand it? I the Lord search the mind and try the heart.*” He sets the sheet down. “Note who’s speaking. The only one in the text who claims to know it is the one I don’t believe in. Mr. Costigan, you have been asked to steal His job. Miss Broussard has merely been asked to agree with Him, which for a Catholic is a dull afternoon.”

“Al-Anfal,” Yusuf says, precise, not looking up from his bridge. “Eight twenty-four. *Know that God comes between a man and his heart.*” He caps his pen. “Which means no one else gets in there either.”
“Selah,” says Caleb.

“No blood today,” Hale says. “It’s midterm week and I am not a monster, only a professor. You will swap, you will bleed on each other by Monday, and I’ll have the corpses at one. Thursday you have my midterm, which will be worse.”
The papers cross the oak. Hers comes to him squared; his goes to her the same way. Their hands don’t come within a foot of each other, and she does it looking at the radiator.
“In the meantime,” Hale says, and leans back until the chair complains. “Mr. Costigan. The Almighty’s job. Tell us how you mean to pull off the burglary.”

choices.text: Answer Hale: Augustine filled ten books with his heart.
response: “Augustine filled ten books with his heart,” Jack says. “For a man who said he couldn’t know it, he took a lot of notes.”
One corner of Hale’s mouth goes up. “And ended in a garden, in tears, certain of nothing but a child’s voice over a wall.” Lena writes something down.

At half past two Lena is first out the door and gone down the cloister without waiting. He reads her paper walking across the Commons, the grass still shining from the storm: “That He Cannot.” Jeremiah 17:9. First Corinthians 4:4. Augustine, *mihi quaestio factus sum*. Thomas, question one-twelve of the *Prima Secundae*: no one knows for certain that he has grace, except by revelation; only by signs, and those conjecturally. Peter at Mark 14:29, *Even though they all fall away, I will not.* O’Connor’s letters. Then the last line, and he stops walking.

response.title: “That He Cannot,” last line
response.text: A woman who says she knows her own heart is either a saint or lying.

body: The TV bolted above the salad bar in Anacapa Commons has been on CNBC since breakfast for reasons the dining staff won’t discuss, and at twenty past six it is still saying it: the Dow closed above ten thousand today, 10,015.86, the first time in a year. Men in blue jackets on the floor of the exchange applaud themselves on a loop over the croutons.
Theo has brought his own Martinelli’s. He fills a plastic cup with it, stands, and raises it to the room. “To capitalism. It came back.”

body.text: “Tell Lordstown,” Jack says. It’s his second Lordstown of the day. The first one got a bigger laugh.

body: His father has been laid off since June. Ohio is pushing ten percent. Whatever came back today hasn’t been told the way to the garage on Glenwood Avenue.
Theo considers this, without irony. “I’ll tell my father,” he says. “He’ll want to option it.”

Laney, in exile at Theo’s table, is eating a waffle with a knife and fork, in small square pieces, with the posture of a girl being judged on it. She has not looked two tables over once, and the effort shows in her neck.

Two tables over, Lena and Margot are sharing a plate of the waffle iron’s bad waffles. Lena is talking with her hands, a fork in one of them, building something in the air over the syrup; Margot is listening with her chin on her fist. Then Margot’s eyes come up and catch Jack looking. Margot looks down at her plate.

By the cereal dispensers the waffle iron beeps for a freshman who has walked away from it, and goes on beeping, and up on the screen the numbers keep climbing in green for people three hours ahead who have already gone home.

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:05 PM · PACIFICA LIBRARY, EIGHTH FLOOR
body: For midterm week the Brick doesn’t close; a sign on an easel in the lobby says so, OPEN 24 HOURS, with a clip-art owl. The eighth floor is the silent floor. Long tables run along the windows, and the windows are black with the post-storm dark, so that the Channel Islands are out there somewhere and might as well not be. At the far end a grad student is asleep under his own coat with one sock showing. Kevin has a table against the stacks, his cards squared by color.

Lena has the window table at the very end: *The Habit of Being*, a steel thermos, a red pen, and Jack’s paper. Jack has a table in the middle of the floor with *The Moviegoer*, the Williams, a red pen and her paper. He is wearing Danny’s Carhartt because the building hasn’t caught up with the weather. Twenty yards of carpet. They haven’t said a word to each other since he came up at eight. Every so often, down at the end, a cap comes off a pen.

The floor smells of carpet glue and wet coats drying on the backs of chairs. The fluorescent tubes hum a note just under hearing, the kind you only notice when it stops. He has her paper open to Aquinas and nothing written beside it yet. He tries Binx instead: *The search is what anyone would undertake if he were not sunk in the everydayness of his own life.* He underlines it, which he did once already in Youngstown in pencil, and now there are two lines under it, gray and red.

At the far end Lena pushes the sleeves of the green sweatshirt up to her elbows, both of them, and bends to his second page with the red pen. He knows what the sleeves mean. He has lost arguments to them since August.

body.text: Are you at the Brick?? Don’t move! :)

body: He texted back *8th floor*, and at five past nine the stairwell door eases open on its slow arm and here she comes: the Marine Lab sweatshirt under her Carhartt vest, the braid down her back still damp from the walk, and a gallon Ziploc held out in front of her. There is a strip of masking tape on it.
Inside: two granola bars, a clementine, a pair of orange foam earplugs, a holy card with the Glory Be on the back, and a square of notebook paper folded in quarters.

Becca has never been in a silent study before, and she whispers like it’s a game with rules and she intends to be very good at it. Then she sees the far end of the room. “Hi, Lena! Good luck!” — a whisper that carries the length of the floor and stirs the grad student’s sock.
She doesn’t stop at that. She crosses the carpet, all twenty yards of it, takes a second clementine out of her vest pocket, and sets it on the table beside Lena’s thermos.
Lena looks up at her. “Thank you, Becca.”

Becca comes back up the carpet, mission accomplished, and bends to Jack’s ear. “I’m asleep by ten,” she whispers. “Farmer.” And she kisses him on the cheek, right there in the silent study, so there’s no confusion, and straightens up, and goes.

response: She turns at the stairwell door. “Really!” she whispers back, thrilled to be whispering, and the door closes behind her on its slow arm.
She turns at the stairwell door with one hand on the push bar. “It’s a *survival* bag, Jack.” As if that settles it. It does. The door closes behind her on its slow arm.

choices.text: “You didn’t have to come all the way over here.”
response: She turns at the stairwell door, surprised he’d think so. “I wanted to see you before I pray.” She says it like a schedule — feed the tank, see Jack, pray, sleep — and the door closes behind her on its slow arm.

s09b.slug: THURSDAY · 12:20 AM · PACIFICA LIBRARY, EIGHTH FLOOR
body: By midnight the eighth floor is two lamps and a sleeping grad student. Two people at two tables, twenty yards apart, marking each other’s arguments in red. The clementine is still on her table by the thermos, unpeeled. His is in the Ziploc with the earplugs. Out past the black glass a few stars have come through where the storm tore the clouds open.

At a quarter past twelve Kevin snaps a last rubber band around a last stack and gets up, and on his way past Jack’s table he stops. He looks down the carpet at the far lamp, and back at Jack, and the big easy smile doesn’t move at all. “Sleep is a study strategy,” he says, and goes down the stairs.

At twenty past, Jack is at her last line. *A woman who says she knows her own heart is either a saint or lying.* He uncaps the red pen and writes beside it, before he can decide not to: *Which are you?*
He caps the pen. He doesn’t look up the room.

At twelve thirty-five he needs air. The elevator takes him down eight floors. At the overnight circulation desk Priya is on her shift in the Fremont High hoodie, shuffling a Ziploc of orgo flashcards for a midterm she took at eight yesterday morning; she doesn’t look up, and he doesn’t make her. Outside the Brick’s doors the concrete is wet and the cold comes straight off the Lagoon, and the eucalyptus are still dripping from the last shower. Under the one working light in the empty lot, Rafi is carving slow circles on his skateboard with his hood up, the wheels hissing on the wet asphalt.
He swings by close. “Boss.” Another lazy circle. “Focus? Midterm special.”

response: Rafi nods like a doctor who has heard worse, and keeps circling.

“No stress,” Rafi says, and pushes off, and the hiss of the wheels goes away across the lot into the dark. Jack rides the elevator back up to the eighth floor, to his table and the carpet and her lamp at the far end of it, and sits under his own lamp until four.

choices.text: “I’m on a Catholic scholarship. We focus through suffering.”
response: Rafi laughs, his head going back under the hood. “My abuela says that. She’s got bad knees, though.”

“No stress,” Rafi says, and pushes off, and the hiss of the wheels goes away across the lot into the dark. Jack rides the elevator back up to the eighth floor, to his table and the carpet and her lamp at the far end of it, and sits under his own lamp until four.
“Not tonight,” Rafi agrees, as if Jack had said something reasonable about the weather.
